title: Ego leaves in good company
hook: in the holy company ego departs and wisdom comes

segments.voice: Yesterday, saadh sangat: in the holy company the face grows bright and the grime washes off. Your line was company shapes you. Today, the same stanza goes deeper, past the face. Day four hundred sixty-four.

Two dinner tables. At the first, one guest talks the whole time: their job, their trip, their opinions. Everyone else nods. At the second, the oldest person there mostly listens, asks good questions, and laughs at other people's stories. Something odd happens at that second table. Nobody tries to win. The loud ones get quieter without being told. By dessert, people are saying things they've never said out loud. Nobody fought anybody's ego. It just left the room. Ashtpadi seven's first stanza has a line about where pride goes in good company.
screen: `ONE GUEST TALKS ALL NIGHT.` → `ANOTHER TABLE, ONE WHO LISTENS.` → `NOBODY FOUGHT THE EGO.`

segments.voice: After the bright face and the washed grime, the stanza continues. Saadh kai sang mitai abhimaan: in the company of the holy, pride is erased. Abhimaan is pride, self-importance, the need to be the one who matters most. Mitai means it's rubbed out, the way chalk disappears from a board. Next line: saadh kai sang pragtai sugiaan. In the holy company, true wisdom shows itself. Sugiaan is good knowing, real understanding. Pragtai means it appears, comes into view, as if it had been there all along, just hidden. And then: in the holy company, God is understood to be near. Notice the order. First pride goes. Then wisdom appears. Then God feels close. Sikh teaching speaks of haumai, the ego that walls the self off, and here is one way the wall comes down: not by attacking it, but by sitting in a place where it has nothing to do. In good company there's no one to compete with, so pride gets bored and wanders off. That's why the carry says quietly. You won't usually notice the moment. You'll just realize, on the way home, that you didn't need to be right tonight, and that you heard something wise you'd have missed if you were talking. One way to live this stanza is to take the listening seat.
screen: `ABHIMAAN: PRIDE, RUBBED OUT.` · `SUGIAAN: WISDOM COMES INTO VIEW.` · `THEN GOD IS FELT NEAR.` · `NOTHING FOR PRIDE TO DO.` · then, large: `EGO LEAVES QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen more than you speak. Start now, with the room you're in. Close your eyes and listen. The nearest sound. The farthest. The sound under all the others. You don't need to name them or judge them. Just receive them. Notice how little of you is needed to listen. Later today, in one conversation, try the same thing: let the other person finish, wait a breath, ask one question instead of telling one story. If you pray, you can listen for the Name in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Abhimaan, pride, self-importance. In the holy company it's rubbed out, and wisdom, sugiaan, comes into view.
Your line: ego leaves quietly. In one conversation today, listen to the end, and ask one question before you say anything about yourself. Day four hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: In the sangat, Sikhs sit together on the floor, without ranked seating, to listen to kirtan and katha; many describe that shared listening as where pride softens.

fork.setup: at a dinner, you have a great story to top everyone else's. by ashtpadi seven, what's the move?
options: listen, and ask a question instead.
fork.reveal: in the holy company pride is rubbed out and wisdom comes into view: the listening seat is where it shows up.

original.note: Gurmukhi: abhimaan, pride or self-importance; the stanza says it is rubbed out in good company.

trapdoor: what you thought: ego leaves when you try hard to be humble.
what it means: in good company pride has nothing to do, and it quietly goes.
what a scholar hears: abhimaan sits beside haumai and ahankaar in Gurbani's vocabulary of ego; the stanza's order is pride erased, wisdom revealed, God known as near.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
